newsitem.title: CUBA: Cuba dismisses U.S. criticism of human rights record.
newsitem.headline: Cuba dismisses U.S. criticism of human rights record.

text.p: Cuba, which views much criticism of its human rights record as part of a political campaign against it by the United States, on Thursday dismissed the latest criticism on the issue from Washington.

Asked about scathing references to Cuba in the State Department's annual review of human rights around the world, Foreign Ministry spokesman Miguel Alfonso said the report should be treated with the importance it deserved -- "practically nil."
Speaking at a regular weekly news briefing, Alfonso reiterated the official view that to treat Cuba as having a particular problem with human rights is a "crude exaggeration."

He added it was traditional that Washington at this time of year make this kind of attack on Cuba, adding the State Department's review of human rights also traditionally had a key omission, human rights in the United States itself.

Alfonso also repeated Havana's stance that Washington attacks Cuba's rights record using its own political criteria. Cuba, a one-party state, argues that examination of human rights issues should also include social rights such as health and education.
The State Department review said the human rights situation on the communist-ruled island worsened in 1996 and suppression of dissent increased. It branded the country a "totalitarian anachronism."

The report followed the release on Tuesday of a White House document that dangles the prospect of billions of dollars of aid and investment to Cuba if the island reforms its political system and dumps President Fidel Castro.
Castro himself attacked the plan in a speech on Tuesday night, saying Cuba was not for sale.

Foreign Minister Roberto Robaina elaborated on Thursday. Cuba was a sovereign state and was not to be sold to the highest bidder, Robaina told Cuban reporters. Cuba long ago took on the risk of living "free and without a price," he added.
